newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official raises human rights with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official raises human rights with China.

text.p: A senior U.S. official raised human rights issues with a Chinese leader in Beijing on Wednesday, hours after a Chinese dissident arrived in the United States seeking asylum, the State Department said.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord, who arrived on Tuesday in Beijing on a previously unannounced visit, had raised Chinese treatment of dissidents at a meeting with Deputy Foreign Minister Liu Huaqiu.
Lord's visit is officially to prepare for a planned trip to Beijing on Nov. 21-22 by Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
"They discussed the situation in Korea, some bilateral issues, including human rights," Burns told a news briefing.

"Human rights have been on our agenda quite importantly over the last couple of days, because of recent arrests of some of the political dissidents, and the recent travel to the United States of a noted champion of human rights. So, that issue for us is front and centre on our agenda with them."

Washington last week sharply criticised the sentencing of dissident Liu Xiaobo to three years in a labour camp, as well as apparent plans to try another pro-democracy activist, Wang Dan, on the capital charge of plotting to subvert the government.

Diplomats in Beijing said China would almost certainly be angered by the arrival of a third dissident, Wang Xizhe, in San Francisco late on Tuesday. Wang fled from China to Hong Kong earlier this week.

Burns said Wang was permitted to enter the United States by Attorney General Janet Reno "because of a very strong fear of persecution should he have remained in China or should he have returned to China once he had left."

Burns declined to say whether Wang had formally requested asylum, but said the U.S. government had decided that Wang should "be given refuge here." He added that he did not foresee any circumstances under which the dissident would be sent back to China.
